grammar.title: Advanced passive forms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Modal + passive**
- Presente/futuro: **modal + be + particípio**: "The results **must be checked**." / "This **could be done** faster."
- Passado: **modal + have been + particípio**: "The sample **must have been contaminated**." / "The disease **could have been prevented**."
- Contínuo (raro): "The data **might be being analysed** right now."

**2. Get passive** (informal) → eventos **inesperados, acidentais** ou **negativos**; também mudança de estado:
- "He **got bitten** by a snake." / "Our flight **got cancelled**." / "She **got promoted**."
- Mais comum na fala; evite em textos acadêmicos.

**3. Have / get something done** (causativo)
- **Serviço** feito por outra pessoa: "I **had** my car **repaired**." / "We need to **get** the samples **analysed**."
- **Experiência negativa** (alguém fez algo com você): "She **had** her bag **stolen**." / "He **had** his application **rejected** three times."

**4. Verbos com dois objetos** (give, send, offer, award, show, lend, tell, promise):
- "They **gave** the scientists a prize." →
  • "The scientists **were given** a prize." (mais comum: pessoa como sujeito)
  • "A prize **was given to** the scientists."

**5. Passiva com preposição no final:**
- "The problem **was dealt with** quickly." / "This theory **has been argued about** for years."

**6. Passiva com verbos de percepção + infinitivo com to:**
- Ativa: "They **saw** him **leave**." → Passiva: "He **was seen to leave**."
- "She **was made to** repeat the experiment." (ativa: They made her repeat...)

pronunciation.focus: must have been / could have been
pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, **must have been** vira "**mâstavbin**" e **could have been** vira "**kúdavbin**". O **been** costuma ser fraco ("bin"). Já em **have something done**, o acento vai no **objeto** e no **particípio**: "I had my **CAR** re**PAIRED**."

dialogue.title: Something went wrong in the lab
dialogue.context_pt: Duas pesquisadoras discutem um resultado inesperado no laboratório.

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: Have you seen these results? They're completely different from last month's.
lines.pt: Você viu esses resultados? São completamente diferentes dos do mês passado.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.en: I have. Either we've made a huge discovery, or something must have gone wrong.
lines.pt: Vi. Ou fizemos uma descoberta enorme, ou alguma coisa deve ter dado errado.

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: My guess is the samples must have been contaminated. Were they stored correctly?
lines.pt: Meu palpite é que as amostras devem ter sido contaminadas. Foram armazenadas corretamente?

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.en: They should have been. But the freezer got switched off during the power cut last week.
lines.pt: Deveriam ter sido. Mas o freezer foi desligado durante a queda de energia semana passada.

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: That could explain it. We'll need to have the remaining samples tested by the external lab.
lines.pt: Isso pode explicar. Vamos precisar mandar testar as amostras restantes no laboratório externo.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.en: I'll get them sent today. And if it was contamination, the whole experiment will have to be repeated.
lines.pt: Vou mandar enviar hoje. E, se foi contaminação, o experimento inteiro vai ter que ser repetido.

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: Let's not panic yet. Remember, penicillin was discovered because a sample got contaminated!
lines.pt: Não vamos entrar em pânico ainda. Lembre-se, a penicilina foi descoberta porque uma amostra foi contaminada!

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.en: True. Maybe we'll be awarded a Nobel Prize for our broken freezer.
lines.pt: Verdade. Talvez a gente ganhe um Nobel pelo nosso freezer quebrado.

listening.title: Science in Brazil
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista científica fala sobre contribuições brasileiras à ciência.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: When people think of great scientific discoveries, Brazil isn't always the first country that comes to mind. Yet Brazilian scientists have made important contributions. In 1909, the physician Carlos Chagas described a new disease — now known as Chagas disease — identifying the parasite that causes it, the insect that transmits it and its clinical symptoms, an achievement that is often described as unique in the history of medicine. The country has also been praised for its agricultural research: Embrapa, the public agricultural research company founded in the 1970s, is widely credited with helping to transform the tropical savannah of the Cerrado into productive farmland — though the environmental costs of that transformation are still debated. And during the Zika outbreak of 2015 and 2016, Brazilian researchers were among the first to establish the link between the virus and microcephaly in newborns. These achievements could not have been made without public funding, which is why cuts to research budgets are a constant concern for the scientific community.

questions.q: What did Carlos Chagas achieve in 1909?
questions.answer: He described a new disease, identifying the parasite, the insect vector and the symptoms.

questions.q: What is Embrapa credited with?
questions.answer: Helping to transform the Cerrado into productive farmland.

questions.q: What link did Brazilian researchers help establish?
questions.answer: The link between the Zika virus and microcephaly.

questions.q: What is a constant concern for scientists?
questions.answer: Cuts to research budgets.

reading.title: The scientist nobody believed
reading.text: For decades, the Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó was considered, by many of her colleagues, to be chasing an impossible dream. Her idea was to use messenger RNA — the molecule that carries genetic instructions inside cells — to make the body produce its own proteins, which could then be used to treat or prevent disease. The problem was that synthetic mRNA, when injected into animals, triggered a strong inflammatory reaction. Grant applications were rejected repeatedly, and in the 1990s she was demoted at the University of Pennsylvania. Most researchers would have given up. Karikó did not. In the early 2000s, working with the immunologist Drew Weissman, she discovered that the inflammatory reaction could be largely avoided if one of the building blocks of the mRNA was slightly modified. Their paper, published in 2005, attracted little attention at the time. Fifteen years later, it was fundamental to one of the fastest medical responses in history. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck, vaccines based on modified mRNA were developed, tested and approved in less than a year — a process that had traditionally taken a decade or more. Hundreds of millions of doses were administered worldwide. In 2023, Karikó and Weissman were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her story is often told as a lesson in persistence. But it also raises uncomfortable questions about the way science is funded. How many other good ideas have been abandoned because they could not be explained in a short grant proposal, or did not produce quick results?

questions.q: What was Karikó's idea?
questions.answer: To use mRNA to make the body produce its own proteins to treat or prevent disease.

questions.q: What was the main problem with synthetic mRNA?
questions.answer: It triggered a strong inflammatory reaction.

questions.q: What did Karikó and Weissman discover?
questions.answer: The reaction could be avoided by slightly modifying one of the mRNA's building blocks.

questions.q: What uncomfortable question does the story raise?
questions.answer: How many good ideas have been abandoned because of the way science is funded?

writing.model:
Ignaz Semmelweis: the doctor who asked for clean hands

In the 1840s, the maternity wards of Vienna General Hospital were divided into two clinics. In the first, women were attended by doctors and medical students; in the second, by midwives. Strangely, the death rate from a condition called childbed fever was far higher in the first clinic. Many mothers begged to be admitted to the second.

The young Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis was determined to find out why. A breakthrough was made in 1847, when a colleague died after being cut accidentally during an autopsy. His symptoms were remarkably similar to those of the dying mothers. Semmelweis concluded that the disease must have been carried by doctors who went straight from dissecting bodies to examining patients.

His solution was simple: all staff were required to have their hands washed in a chlorine solution before touching patients. The results were dramatic. Within months, the death rate in the first clinic had fallen sharply.

Yet his ideas were not welcomed. Many senior doctors were offended by the suggestion that they themselves could be responsible for their patients' deaths. Germ theory had not yet been developed, so his findings could not be fully explained. Semmelweis was not given a permanent position, and he eventually left Vienna.

His later years were tragic. His behaviour became increasingly erratic, and in 1865 he was committed to an asylum, where he died shortly afterwards, apparently after being beaten by guards.

Only years later, after the work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister, was Semmelweis recognized as a pioneer of antiseptic practice. Today he is often called "the saviour of mothers". His story is a painful reminder that good evidence can be ignored when it challenges powerful people — and that many lives might have been saved if he had been listened to.

culture_note.title: "Publish or perish"
culture_note.text_pt: No mundo acadêmico anglófono, a expressão **"publish or perish"** (publique ou pereça) resume a pressão sobre pesquisadores para publicar artigos constantemente. Críticos dizem que isso incentiva pesquisas rápidas e "seguras" em vez de ideias arriscadas — como as de Katalin Karikó, que levaram décadas para dar frutos.

grammar.title: The subjunctive and formal structures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Subjuntivo presente** = **verbo base** para **todas as pessoas** (sem -s, sem do, sem tempo passado).
Aparece depois de verbos e adjetivos de **exigência, recomendação ou importância**:
- Verbos: **recommend, suggest, insist, demand, propose, request, require, ask, urge** + **that**
- Adjetivos: **it is essential / vital / crucial / important / necessary / imperative that**

"The doctor **recommended that** she **take** a break." (não "takes")
"They **insisted that** the trial **be** stopped." (não "is" / "was")
"It is **vital that** he **not** be informed yet." (negativa: **not** + base)

⚠️ O tempo do verbo principal **não muda** o subjuntivo: "They **demanded** that he **resign**."

**Alternativa britânica (menos formal):** **should** + verbo: "They recommended that the study **should be** suspended." Ambas são corretas.

**2. Should no lugar de if (inversão)** — hipóteses educadas e formais:
- "**Should you need** any further information, do not hesitate to contact us." (= If you need...)

**3. Were it not for / Had it not been for** (= se não fosse por):
- "**Were it not for** vaccines, millions more would die every year."
- "**Had it not been for** the transplant, he would have died."

**4. Expressões fixas com subjuntivo** (muito comuns!):
- **Be that as it may** (seja como for)
- **Come what may** (aconteça o que acontecer)
- **God save the King / Long live...**
- **Suffice it to say** (basta dizer)
- **If need be** (se for necessário)
- **So be it** (que assim seja)
- **..., be it X or Y** (seja X ou Y): "All life, **be it** human or animal, deserves respect."

dialogue.title: The ethics committee
dialogue.context_pt: Uma reunião de comitê de ética avalia uma proposta de pesquisa genética (situação fictícia).

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: Let's move on to the gene therapy proposal. Dr. Lima, could you summarize your concerns?
lines.pt: Vamos para a proposta de terapia gênica. Dr. Lima, poderia resumir suas preocupações?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: Certainly. The science is promising, but I would recommend that the trial be limited to adult patients at first.
lines.pt: Claro. A ciência é promissora, mas eu recomendaria que o ensaio fosse limitado a pacientes adultos inicialmente.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: And informed consent?
lines.pt: E o consentimento informado?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: That's my main point. It is essential that every participant fully understand the risks. Some of these patients are desperate, and desperation can affect judgement.
lines.pt: Esse é meu ponto principal. É essencial que cada participante entenda plenamente os riscos. Alguns desses pacientes estão desesperados, e o desespero pode afetar o julgamento.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: With respect, were it not for trials like this, these patients would have no hope at all. Delaying it also has a cost.
lines.pt: Com todo o respeito, não fossem ensaios como este, esses pacientes não teriam esperança nenhuma. Adiar também tem um custo.

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: Be that as it may, we have a duty to protect them. I'd also insist that an independent team monitor the results.
lines.pt: Seja como for, temos o dever de protegê-los. Eu também insistiria que uma equipe independente monitorasse os resultados.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: That's reasonable. Should any serious side effects appear, the trial could be stopped immediately.
lines.pt: Isso é razoável. Caso surjam efeitos colaterais graves, o ensaio poderia ser interrompido imediatamente.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: So, I propose that we approve the trial, subject to those two conditions. All in favour?
lines.pt: Então, proponho que aprovemos o ensaio, sujeito a essas duas condições. Todos a favor?

listening.title: The CRISPR babies
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista científica relata o caso dos bebês editados geneticamente na China.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: In November 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced that he had used the gene-editing tool CRISPR to alter the DNA of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls. His stated aim was to make them resistant to HIV. The reaction from the scientific community was almost universally negative. Critics argued that the procedure was medically unnecessary, that its long-term effects were unknown, and that the changes could be passed on to future generations. Many questioned whether the parents had given truly informed consent. He was later sentenced to prison in China. The case led to calls from leading scientists that a global moratorium be placed on heritable genome editing until its safety and ethics could be properly assessed. It's worth noting that gene editing in non-reproductive cells — which only affects the patient — is a different matter, and therapies of this kind have already been approved in some countries. The line, most experts agree, is crossed when changes are made that will be inherited.

questions.q: What did He Jiankui announce in 2018?
questions.answer: He had edited the DNA of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls.

questions.q: Name two criticisms of the procedure.
questions.answer: It was medically unnecessary / long-term effects unknown / changes could be inherited / doubts about consent.

questions.q: What did leading scientists call for?
questions.answer: A global moratorium on heritable genome editing.

questions.q: Where is the line crossed, according to most experts?
questions.answer: When changes are made that will be inherited.

reading.title: Who decides?
reading.text: Few technologies have raised hopes and fears as dramatically as gene editing. Tools such as CRISPR, whose developers Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, allow scientists to modify DNA with a precision that would have been unimaginable a generation ago. The potential benefits are enormous. Inherited diseases that have caused suffering for centuries could, in theory, be corrected. In 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first therapy based on CRISPR, designed to treat sickle cell disease. Yet the same technology raises profound ethical questions. If it becomes possible to eliminate a disease, should it also be possible to select for height, intelligence or appearance? Critics warn of a slippery slope towards "designer babies" and a world in which genetic advantages are available only to the wealthy. Disability rights advocates have also asked who gets to decide which human traits count as "defects". Most scientific bodies currently insist that a clear distinction be maintained between somatic editing, which affects only the individual patient, and germline editing, whose changes would be inherited by future generations. The first is increasingly accepted; the second remains, in most countries, prohibited. But laws vary from one country to another, and technology tends to move faster than regulation. Were it not for international cooperation, the rules could easily be bypassed by researchers moving to countries with weaker oversight. Perhaps the most important question is not what science can do, but who should decide what it ought to do — scientists, governments, patients or society as a whole. Be that as it may, it seems essential that these decisions not be left to a few laboratories alone.

questions.q: Who developed CRISPR and what were they awarded?
questions.answer: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier; the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

questions.q: What was approved in 2023?
questions.answer: The first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease (UK and US).

questions.q: What is the difference between somatic and germline editing?
questions.answer: Somatic affects only the patient; germline changes are inherited.

questions.q: Why is international cooperation important?
questions.answer: Otherwise researchers could move to countries with weaker oversight.

writing.task: Write a formal essay (280–320 words): "Gene editing should be used only to treat disease, never to enhance human abilities." Discuss both sides and give your opinion. Use at least four subjunctive forms and two other formal structures from this lesson.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma redação formal (280–320 palavras): "A edição genética deveria ser usada apenas para tratar doenças, nunca para melhorar capacidades humanas." Discuta os dois lados e dê sua opinião. Use pelo menos quatro formas de subjuntivo e duas outras estruturas formais da aula.
writing.model:
Treatment or enhancement? The limits of gene editing

Advances in gene-editing technology have made it possible, for the first time in history, to alter human DNA with remarkable precision. While few would object to its use in curing devastating diseases, many experts insist that a firm line be drawn between treatment and enhancement. This essay will examine whether such a line is both desirable and realistic.

The case for restricting gene editing to medical treatment is a strong one. Were it not for clear limits, the technology could easily be used to create genetic advantages for those who could afford them, deepening existing inequalities. Moreover, our understanding of the human genome remains incomplete. A change intended to improve one characteristic might have unforeseen consequences elsewhere, and if made in embryos, those consequences would be inherited by future generations. It is therefore vital that any intervention be justified by a serious medical need.

On the other hand, critics argue that the distinction between treatment and enhancement is far from clear. Is strengthening the immune system a treatment or an enhancement? What about reducing the risk of a condition that may never develop? Some have also pointed out that we already accept many forms of enhancement, from vaccines to education, and that refusing genetic improvements on principle may be inconsistent.

Be that as it may, I believe the risks of allowing enhancement currently outweigh the potential benefits. The technology is too new, its long-term effects too uncertain and its social consequences too unpredictable. I would therefore recommend that its use be limited to the treatment of serious diseases, and that any change to that policy be decided through public debate rather than by scientists or companies alone. Should our knowledge improve significantly in the future, the question could be reconsidered. Until then, caution seems the wisest course.

grammar.title: Describing data and academic hedging
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Descrevendo tendências** — duas estruturas equivalentes:
- **Verbo + advérbio:** "Sales **rose sharply**." / "Prices **fell slightly**."
- **Adjetivo + substantivo:** "There was **a sharp rise** in sales." / "**a slight fall** in prices."

**Verbos:** rise, increase, grow, climb, **soar**, **rocket** ↗ · fall, decrease, drop, decline, **plummet**, **plunge** ↘ · **fluctuate** ↕ · **level off**, **stabilize**, remain steady → · **peak**, reach a high/low
**Advérbios/adjetivos de intensidade:** dramatically, sharply, significantly, considerably, steadily, gradually, slightly, marginally

**Preposições** (erro comum!):
- rose **from** 10% **to** 25% · rose **by** 15 percentage points · **a** rise **in** prices · **a** rise **of** 15% · peaked **at** 30%

**Multiplicadores:** doubled / tripled / a **threefold** increase / **twice as many as** / **three times as high as**

**2. Aproximações:**
- **just over / just under / roughly / approximately / around / nearly / almost**
- **the vast majority / a significant minority / a small proportion / one in five / a quarter**

**3. Hedging acadêmico** (suavizar quando a evidência é limitada):
- Verbos: **appear to, seem to, tend to, suggest, indicate**
- Modais: **may, might, could**
- Expressões: **it would appear that / there is evidence to suggest that / to some extent / in some cases / it is likely that**
- Advérbios: **possibly, probably, arguably, apparently**

Compare:
- Forte demais: "Social media **causes** depression."
- Acadêmico: "There **is some evidence to suggest** that heavy social media use **may be associated with** higher rates of depression."

**Boosters** (quando a evidência é forte): clearly, undoubtedly, it is evident that, the data **demonstrate**.

examples.en: The number of internet users in Brazil rose steadily throughout the 2010s, reaching the vast majority of the population by the end of the decade.

grammar.tip_pt: Atenção à diferença: **percent** (%) x **percentage points**. Se a taxa de desemprego vai de 10% para 12%, ela subiu **2 percentage points** — mas aumentou **20 percent** em termos relativos. Jornalistas confundem isso o tempo todo!

pronunciation.tip_pt: Atenção: **thirty** (30) x **thirteen** (13) — em **thirTEEN** o acento cai no final; em **THIRty**, no começo. **Percent** = "per-SÉNT". Decimais: **2.5** = "two point five" (ponto, não vírgula!). Datas: **2019** = "twenty nineteen".

listening.title: Describing a graph
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de IELTS mostra como descrever um gráfico sobre o uso de bicicletas (dados fictícios criados para a aula).

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Let's look at this example. The line graph shows the number of daily bicycle trips in a fictional city between 2010 and 2025. Overall, cycling increased dramatically over the period, although there were some fluctuations. In 2010, there were roughly 20,000 daily trips. This figure remained fairly stable until 2014, when the city opened its first network of cycle lanes. Over the following four years, the number of trips more than doubled, reaching just over 45,000 in 2018. There was a sharp fall in 2020, when trips plummeted to around 25,000, which would appear to be linked to lockdown restrictions. However, the figure recovered rapidly, peaking at approximately 60,000 in 2023 — a threefold increase compared with 2010 — before levelling off. Notice what I did there: an overview first, then the key figures, and a careful "would appear to be linked" — because the graph alone can't prove the cause.

questions.q: Why does the teacher use "would appear to be linked"?

reading.title: How to lie with statistics
reading.text: In 1954, the American writer Darrell Huff published a small book with a provocative title: How to Lie with Statistics. Despite its age, many of its warnings remain remarkably relevant. Perhaps the most common trap is confusing correlation with causation. Countries that consume more chocolate per person, for example, tend to have won more Nobel Prizes per capita — a correlation highlighted, half-jokingly, in a 2012 article in a medical journal. Few would seriously conclude that chocolate makes people smarter. A far more likely explanation is that both are associated with a third factor: national wealth. Yet similar reasoning appears regularly in headlines about diet, technology and health. A second trap involves relative and absolute risk. A headline announcing that a medicine "doubles the risk" of a side effect sounds alarming. But if the risk rises from one in 10,000 to two in 10,000, the absolute increase is tiny. Both statements are technically true; only one gives the reader a fair picture. Third, there is the problem of the sample. A survey of 200 enthusiastic app users cannot tell us much about the population as a whole, however impressive its results may appear. Finally, graphs themselves can mislead. By starting the vertical axis at a number other than zero, a designer can make a marginal change look dramatic. None of this means that statistics are useless — quite the opposite. Used carefully, they are among the most powerful tools we have for understanding the world. The point is that numbers, like words, need to be read critically. As a rule of thumb, it would seem wise to ask three questions of any statistic: compared to what, measured how, and according to whom?

questions.q: What is the chocolate example meant to show?
questions.answer: That correlation doesn't imply causation (both linked to national wealth).

questions.q: What is the difference between relative and absolute risk in the example?
questions.answer: "Doubles" sounds big, but the absolute rise is only from 1 to 2 in 10,000.

questions.q: How can graphs mislead?
questions.answer: By starting the vertical axis at a number other than zero.

questions.q: What three questions does the writer suggest asking?

The bar chart illustrates the proportion of commuters in a large Brazilian city who travelled to work by car, public transport and bicycle in 2005, 2015 and 2025. (The figures are fictional.)

Overall, public transport remained the most common way of commuting throughout the period, while cycling, although still a minority choice, grew considerably. The use of cars, by contrast, rose and then fell.

In 2005, just over half of commuters (52%) used public transport, compared with roughly a third (34%) who drove. Only a very small proportion — around 2% — cycled to work. Over the following decade, car use increased to 41%, which would appear to reflect the rise in car ownership during that period, while the share of public transport fell slightly to 47%.

Between 2015 and 2025, however, this trend was reversed. The proportion of car commuters fell sharply to 30%, whereas public transport recovered to 50%. Most strikingly, cycling more than tripled, reaching 7% by 2025. This increase may be linked to the expansion of cycle lanes, although other factors, such as the growth of shared bicycles, could also account for it.

In summary, the data suggest a gradual shift towards more sustainable forms of transport in recent years.

grammar.title: Advanced concession
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. However / Whatever / Whoever / Wherever / Whenever + oração** (= não importa como/o que/quem...)
- **However + adjetivo/advérbio + S + V**: "**However hard** I try, I can't understand it." / "**However much** it costs, we'll pay."
- "**Whatever** you decide, I'll support you." / "**Whoever** wins, the country will be divided."
- Com **may** (mais formal): "**However** difficult it **may** be, ..."

**2. No matter + what / how / who / where / when**
- "**No matter how** many times I explain, he doesn't listen." (≈ However many times...)
- "**No matter what** happens, stay calm."

**3. Adjetivo / advérbio + though / as + S + V** (formal, enfático):
- "**Difficult though** it is, we must decide." / "**Tempting as** it may be, we should not lie."

**4. Concessão com advérbios e expressões** (reconhecer → contrapor):
- **Admittedly**, ... / **Granted**, ... / **It is true that** ..., **but** ...
- **While it is true that** ..., ... / **Although it may be argued that** ..., ...
- **Be that as it may**, ... / **Even so**, ... / **All the same**, ... / **That said**, ...
- "**Admittedly**, lying can sometimes protect people. **Even so**, I believe honesty is the better policy in the long run."

**5. Much as / However much** (revisão da M1-L3): "**Much as** I admire her, I can't agree."

**Estrutura de argumento concessivo:**
**reconhecer** (Admittedly / Granted / While it is true that...) → **contrapor** (However / Even so / Be that as it may) → **reforçar a sua posição**.

dialogue.title: The self-driving dilemma
dialogue.context_pt: Dois engenheiros discutem como programar um carro autônomo para situações de acidente inevitável.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.en: Here's the scenario we have to program for: the brakes fail, and the car must either hit a group of pedestrians or swerve into a wall, possibly killing the passenger.
lines.pt: Este é o cenário para o qual precisamos programar: os freios falham, e o carro precisa atingir um grupo de pedestres ou desviar para um muro, possivelmente matando o passageiro.

lines.speaker: Ellen
lines.en: Mathematically, it's simple — one life versus several. The car should swerve.
lines.pt: Matematicamente, é simples — uma vida contra várias. O carro deveria desviar.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.en: Admittedly, that saves more lives. But who would buy a car that might decide to kill them?
lines.pt: É verdade que isso salva mais vidas. Mas quem compraria um carro que pode decidir matá-lo?

lines.speaker: Ellen
lines.en: Fair point. Even so, whatever we program, someone will be harmed. We can't avoid the choice.
lines.pt: Bom argumento. Mesmo assim, o que quer que programemos, alguém sairá ferido. Não podemos evitar a escolha.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.en: Granted. But however carefully we design the rules, real accidents are messier than thought experiments.
lines.pt: Concordo. Mas, por mais cuidadosamente que desenhemos as regras, acidentes reais são mais complicados que experimentos mentais.

lines.speaker: Ellen
lines.en: True. Strange though it sounds, the best answer might be to focus on making these situations almost impossible — better sensors, slower speeds in cities.
lines.pt: Verdade. Por mais estranho que pareça, a melhor resposta talvez seja focar em tornar essas situações quase impossíveis — sensores melhores, velocidades menores nas cidades.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.en: I agree. Be that as it may, the regulators still want an answer for the rare cases.
lines.pt: Concordo. Seja como for, os reguladores ainda querem uma resposta para os casos raros.

lines.speaker: Ellen
lines.en: Then we can't sit on the fence. Let's present both options with the data — and let society decide.
lines.pt: Então não podemos ficar em cima do muro. Vamos apresentar as duas opções com os dados — e deixar a sociedade decidir.

listening.title: The Moral Machine
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora apresenta os resultados de um grande experimento online sobre dilemas morais.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: In 2016, researchers at MIT launched an online experiment called the Moral Machine. It presented visitors with variations of the famous trolley problem, adapted for self-driving cars: should the car save its passengers or the pedestrians? The young or the elderly? More lives or fewer? Millions of people from over two hundred countries and territories took part, and the results were published in Nature in 2018. Some preferences were broadly shared: in general, people chose to spare more lives rather than fewer, humans rather than animals, and the young rather than the old. But there were also notable cultural differences. Participants from some regions, for example, showed a weaker preference for sparing younger people. Whatever you think of the method — and it has been criticized for oversimplifying real situations — the study raises a difficult question. However universal our moral instincts may seem, they may not be the same everywhere. So whose values should a machine follow?

questions.q: What did the Moral Machine present to visitors?
questions.answer: Variations of the trolley problem adapted for self-driving cars.

questions.q: How many people took part, roughly?
questions.answer: Millions, from over 200 countries and territories.

questions.q: Name two broadly shared preferences.
questions.answer: Sparing more lives, humans over animals, the young over the old.

questions.q: What criticism of the method is mentioned?
questions.answer: It oversimplifies real situations.

reading.title: Is it ever right to lie?
reading.text: Few moral questions are as old, or as practical, as this one. The eighteenth-century philosopher Immanuel Kant took an uncompromising position. Lying, he argued, is always wrong, whatever the consequences — even, in a much-debated example, when a murderer comes to your door asking where your friend is hiding. However extreme this may sound, Kant's reasoning was that a lie treats other people as mere instruments and undermines the trust on which all communication depends. Most people find this conclusion hard to accept. Admittedly, honesty is a value almost every culture shares. Even so, few of us believe we should tell a friend that their wedding speech was boring, or tell a terrified patient every grim statistic at once. Consequentialist philosophers, following thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, argue that the morality of an action depends on its outcomes. If a lie prevents serious harm, it may be not only permissible but right. Yet this view has its own difficulties. Who decides which consequences matter, and how far ahead must we look? A "white lie" that spares someone's feelings today may damage their trust tomorrow. Psychologists add an interesting twist. Research suggests that most of us lie more often than we think, and that we tend to judge our own lies far more generously than those of others. Much as we may admire honesty in principle, our everyday behaviour is more complicated. Perhaps the most realistic answer is that honesty is a strong default, not an absolute rule. Granted, that leaves us with grey areas. But moral life, whatever philosophers may wish, has always been full of them.

questions.q: What was Kant's position on lying?
questions.answer: Lying is always wrong, whatever the consequences.

questions.q: Why did Kant believe this?
questions.answer: A lie treats people as instruments and undermines trust.

questions.q: What do consequentialists argue?
questions.answer: The morality of an action depends on its outcomes.

questions.q: What does research suggest about how we judge lies?
questions.answer: We judge our own lies more generously than others'.

writing.task: Write a discursive essay (280–320 words): "Is it ever right to break the law?" Present both sides, use at least five concessive structures and reach a clear conclusion.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma redação discursiva (280–320 palavras): "É certo, em alguma situação, desobedecer à lei?" Apresente os dois lados, use pelo menos cinco estruturas concessivas e chegue a uma conclusão clara.
writing.model:
Is it ever right to break the law?

In a democratic society, laws are meant to reflect shared values and protect citizens. It might therefore seem obvious that they should always be obeyed. However, history offers numerous examples of people who broke the law and are now remembered as heroes. This essay will consider whether breaking the law can ever be justified.

There are strong arguments for obeying the law in all circumstances. If individuals could ignore any law they disagreed with, the result would be chaos. Whatever our personal views, the rule of law protects the weak from the strong and allows disagreements to be resolved peacefully. Admittedly, laws are sometimes unjust. Even so, democratic societies offer legal ways of changing them, such as elections, protests and the courts.

On the other hand, it is difficult to argue that every law deserves obedience. Rosa Parks broke the law when she refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, yet few people today would say she was wrong. However legitimate a government may appear, its laws can still be deeply immoral, and legal routes to change can be slow or blocked entirely. In such cases, peaceful civil disobedience may be the only way to draw attention to injustice.

Granted, the line between principled disobedience and simple law-breaking is not always clear. Much as we may admire activists, we should be wary of anyone who claims the right to decide which laws apply to them.

In conclusion, I believe that breaking the law can be justified, but only in exceptional circumstances: when the law is clearly unjust, when legal options have been exhausted, and when the act is peaceful and open, with the person willing to accept the consequences. Difficult though it may be to define these limits precisely, they distinguish conscience from mere convenience.

culture_note.title: O "trolley problem"
culture_note.text_pt: O famoso **trolley problem** (problema do bonde) foi formulado pela filósofa britânica **Philippa Foot** em 1967 e popularizado depois por **Judith Jarvis Thomson**. Virou meme na internet e ganhou nova relevância com os carros autônomos. Em inglês, dizer que algo é "a real trolley problem" significa que todas as opções têm um custo moral.
